title: Reading Files 📖
description: Master the essential file viewers: cat, less, head, tail, and wc to inspect any text.

slides.title: Your Reading Toolkit 🔧
slides.content:
## Bash is a Text Powerhouse

Most system data is plain text: logs, configs, CSV exports. Before modifying anything, you need to **view** it safely. Bash offers a suite of commands for exactly that.

Today's stars:
- `cat` – concatenate and print entire files
- `less` – scroll through large files
- `head` / `tail` – peek at the beginning or end
- `wc` – count lines, words, and bytes

slides.title: cat: Dump It All 🐱
slides.content: `cat` displays the full content of one or more files. Great for small files, dangerous for huge ones.

quizData.question: What does `cat file1 file2` do?
quizData.explanation: `cat` concatenates and prints all given files in order.

slides.title: less: Scroll with Ease 📜
slides.content: `less` opens a file in a pager. Use arrows, PgUp/Down, `/` to search, `q` to quit.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Inside `less`, press `G` to jump to the end, `g` to go to the top, and `-N` flag shows line numbers (`less -N file`).

slides.title: head & tail: First & Last Glimpses 🔭
slides.content:
## Peek Without Opening Fully

- `head -n 5 file` – first 5 lines (default 10).
- `tail -n 5 file` – last 5 lines.
- `tail -f file` – follow; continuously show new lines (great for logs).

quizData.question: Which `tail` option keeps watching a file for new lines?
quizData.explanation: `tail -f` follows the file, showing appended data in real time.

slides.title: wc: Count Everything 🔢
slides.content:
`wc` prints line, word, and byte counts.
- `-l` : lines only
- `-w` : words only
- `-c` : bytes only

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `wc -l < file` to avoid printing the filename, or pipe `cat file | wc -l`.
